fixes.explanation: A threshing floor is where grain gets worked, and Ahab never mentions one. He says he wants the vineyard “…to use as a vegetable garden…” The only reason he gives is that it's next to his palace. It's an easy mix-up with all that farm talk, and I once mixed up salt and sugar, so I'm in no position to judge.

Olives are a fair guess, but the king never says a word about them. His plan is the vineyard “…to use as a vegetable garden…” He also points out that it's right next to his palace. A king with a whole palace and his heart set on a vegetable patch, and not one olive on his wish list.

Silver it is, baker. Ahab gives Naboth two choices: a better vineyard in its place, or if Naboth prefers, the vineyard's value in silver. Naboth is the vineyard's owner, and he answers, “The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers.” Ahab's offer had more options than my old 25 cent price sticker ever did.

Cattle never come up. The king offers Naboth a better vineyard in its place, or if Naboth prefers, its value in silver. Paying for a vineyard with a herd would've meant a whole lot of mooing on the way to the palace.
Eat is right, baker. Ahab lies down on his bed, turns his face away and refuses to eat. I'd wave a cookie under his nose, but I think this one needed more than that.
Ahab's face is turned away, but the text never says he refuses to speak. When Jezebel asks what's wrong, he answers her and tells her all about Naboth (1 Kings 21:6). The thing he refuses is food.

An apology is small stuff next to what she promises. Jezebel, Ahab's wife, says, “…I will get you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.” She skips right past sorry and goes for the whole vineyard. That's a bold way to cheer up a sulking husband.

True, baker. Jezebel writes the letters in Ahab's name, seals them with his seal, and sends them to the elders and nobles who lived with Naboth in his city. Jezebel wrote them, but they carry Ahab's name and Ahab's seal. The leaders of Naboth's city got letters that looked like they came from the king.

It's true, though. The text says Jezebel wrote the letters in Ahab's name, sealed them with his seal, and sent them to the elders and nobles who lived with Naboth in his city. Those leaders are the ones the letters were sent to.
No soldiers here either. Jezebel's letters say to “…seat two scoundrels opposite him…” (1 Kings 21:10) Scoundrels are the word the text uses for those two men.

It's true, sadly. The text says the elders and nobles of Naboth's city “…did as Jezebel had instructed in the letters she had written to them.” (1 Kings 21:11) They carried out what the letters said. This is a heavy part of the story.

No burial comes up in her words. Jezebel, Ahab's wife, tells him, “Get up and take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite…” She does say Naboth is dead, but she never mentions a burial. What she points Ahab to is the vineyard.

Silver does come up, but not as payment. Jezebel says Naboth “…refused to give it to you for silver.” Her order to Ahab is “Get up and take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite…” Nothing in that order says to pay Naboth's family.

The elders aren't part of Elijah's orders. The LORD tells Elijah the Tishbite, God's prophet, “Get up and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria.” The instruction names one person to meet, and that's Ahab.

That's the message. The LORD says, “In the place where the dogs licked up the blood of Naboth, there also the dogs will lick up your blood…” He names the place where the dogs licked up Naboth's blood, and says Ahab's blood will be licked up there too. It's a heavy word, baker.

True. After Ahab says, “So you have found me out, my enemy.” Elijah replies, “I have found you out because you have sold yourself to do evil in the sight of the LORD.” Elijah gives the reason straight.

That's the reason, baker. The LORD says, “…because you have provoked My anger and caused Israel to sin.” (1 Kings 21:22) Jeroboam son of Nebat and Baasha son of Ahijah are the two houses He compares Ahab's to. The LORD gives His reason, and it's about Ahab's own actions.

Sackcloth, baker. The text says Ahab “…tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and fasted.” Ahab heard every word from Elijah, and then he acted. This is the same king who called Elijah his enemy earlier in this passage.
